title: About
text:
I spent 12 years in asset management, working with quantitative models, data, uncertainty and investment portfolios.
Over time, I found myself increasingly drawn to the mathematics and mechanics underneath the decisions: how models represent the world, what information they capture, and where their assumptions begin to break down.
That curiosity eventually led me to step away from finance and pursue an MSc in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Science. I am now preparing to begin a PhD and continue exploring the relationship between mathematics, machine learning and scientific inference.
I enjoy trying to understand technical ideas from first principles and finding ways to make their underlying structure easier to see. I do not think difficult subjects need to be made artificially simple, but I do think they can often be explained more clearly.
My current interests include scientific machine learning and inverse problems. More broadly, I am interested in what models can learn from data, what remains unidentifiable, and how visualisation can help expose both the strengths and limitations of a model.
I am still learning, and I expect my understanding of many of these subjects to change. Part of the reason for building this site is to document that process.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
A gravitational-wave signal is an observation of a source, not a direct description of it.
Different combinations of source parameters can sometimes produce very similar observed signals.
That makes gravitational-wave inference an inverse problem: we observe the waveform and try to infer the system that produced it.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
The basic idea
Suppose we observe a reference waveform.
We then vary two source parameters and compare the resulting candidate waveform with the reference.
Some combinations may look noticeably different.
Others may be surprisingly similar.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
A degeneracy
If many different parameter combinations produce nearly the same observation, the inverse problem does not have one obvious answer.
Instead, there can be a region of parameter space where many solutions are plausible.
That structure is often described as a parameter degeneracy.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
section: Why this matters for machine learning
text:
Why this matters for machine learning
A model can only infer what is present in the data.
If two physically different systems produce almost indistinguishable observations, a more complicated model does not automatically solve the problem.
The ambiguity is partly in the data itself.

title: When different black-hole binaries look the same
text:
Breaking the degeneracy
More information can help.
Longer observations, additional waveform structure or richer detector information may distinguish systems that initially looked equivalent.
The interesting question is therefore not only:
What can the model learn?
but also:
What does the observation make possible to learn in the first place?

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
“This survey is anonymous.”
That sounds binary: either your identity is known, or it is not.
But anonymity is better thought of as a budget.
Every piece of information you reveal narrows the set of people you could be. Some answers spend very little of that budget. Others spend a lot.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
One bit at a time
A bit can be thought of as one perfectly chosen yes-or-no question that cuts the remaining group in half.
In a company of 500 people, there are only about nine halvings between the whole company and one person.
That does not mean nine survey questions will automatically identify you. Real surveys involve aggregation, imperfect information and organisational safeguards.
But it gives us a useful way to think about how quickly information accumulates.

title: Anonymity is not binary
Anonymity is not binary
text:
Rarity changes the cost
Not every answer reveals the same amount.
If half the company gives the same answer as you, that answer costs about one bit.
If only 1% of the company shares your answer, it reveals much more.
That means the same dropdown can have a very different anonymity cost for different respondents.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
Why demographics are difficult
Demographic information is often the most revealing part of a survey.
It is also often the information needed to detect inequities.
That creates a genuine tension: the groups whose experiences matter most to measure can also be the groups that are easiest to identify.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
What this does not mean
Being identifiable in principle is not the same as being identified, and being identified is not the same as being harmed.
Trust, governance, aggregation thresholds and organisational culture all matter.
The point is simpler: anonymity is not a switch. It is something that erodes as information accumulates.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
A useful consequence
If only a small minority raises an issue, the issue itself can become identifying information.
When more people raise the same genuine concern, that link weakens.
In that sense, anonymity can sometimes be strengthened collectively: when enough people say the true thing, no single voice stands out.

title: Anonymity is not binary
text:
What this calculator assumes
This is an illustration, not a re-identification tool.
The calculator assumes that the attributes you enter are independent, so it multiplies their population shares together. Real workplaces are messier: seniority, location, tenure and demographic characteristics can be correlated, sometimes strongly.
The resulting “people remaining” number should therefore be read as a simple expected count under that assumption, not as the number of people who could actually be identified.
It also ignores many things that matter in practice: aggregation thresholds, suppression of small groups, access controls, free-text responses, prior knowledge and the policies governing who can see the data.
The useful quantity here is the information revealed by a combination of answers, rather than a claim that a particular survey respondent can or will be identified.
